451147,ca.proc.d.1916-04-27.3.5.2,1916-04-27,b2723513-c609-4a5c-87f4-bd7c225ccd75,ca.m.2309,Mr. H. H. STEVENS (Vancouver):,,QUESTIONS.,ALLEGED ENLISTMENT OP FOREIGN LABOURERS.,,I would like to draw the attention of the Government, particularly of the Minister of the Interior, to a rather serious matter in connection with a statement alleged to have been made by the American Consul in Vancouver. I shall read a despatch from Portland, Oregon, that appears in a Vancouver paper, which will explain the situation pretty fully:

Portland, Ore., April 18.-The charge that American labourers are being induced to migrate to Canada on the promise of lucrative employment and then are forced by the pressure of the authorities and of the circumstances by which they find themselves surrounded to enlist in Great Britain's overseas army, is made by the United States Department of Labour Bureau of Immigration in a bulletin which was issued here to-day by the local immigration commissioner.
Quoting from the report of the American consul-general at Vancouver, B.C., the bulletin says:

Special efforts are being made to induce every foreigner of military age to enlist for the overseas service and it is practically impossible for an American to secure employment in any capacity. Several thousands of Americans have gone from British Columbia to the United States during the past year, a majority of whom went for the reason they were unable to do business or secure employment and some because of the endeavour on the part of the authorities to enlist them for military service.""

Then the grossly false and misleading statement is made that thousands of men are idle in Vancouver, and that a propaganda is being carried on in the United States to induce Americans to emigrate to Canada for the ostensible purpose of securing employment, etc. The statement made by this American Consul-General at Vancouver that the Canadian military authorities are using undud pressure to force foreigners to serve in what he calls Britain's overseas army I characterize as absolutely false. I wish to draw the attention of the Government to this statement, and to the indignation of the people, particularly of my own city of Vancouver, in regard to the matter. An editorial appearing in the Vancouver World of April 19, referring to this despatch, is in part as follows:
There is only one course for the citizens of British Columbia to pursue in the case of Mr. Rjbrt E. Mansfield, the American consul here -that is demand his immediate recall.
In asserting that American labourers are being induced to come to Canada on the promise of lucrative employment and are then

forced by "" pressure of the authorities "" to enlist in what he ' erroneously styles "" Great Britain's Overseas Army,"" the American consul states what is absolutely false, what he must know to be false and what is an insult to every true Canadian. The World yesterday invited Mr. Mansfield to explain his assertion, but he declared he had ""nothing to say.""
* So far from labourers being invited to enter British Columbia, they have been specifically barred out.

The American Consul knows this fact as well as any one. That he should make such a statement as ""a propaganda is being carried on through the press and other channels in the United States to induce Americans to migrate to Canada for the ostensible purpose of securing employment "", but really in order to be pressed into "" Great Britain's Overseas' Army "", is so preposterous that it carries its own refutation with it.

The people of Canada-and of British Columbia in particular-are always glad to welcome the official representatives of our great neighbour to the South. Almost without exception they have upheld the traditions of their office and conducted their affairs with fairness and courtesy. It has been left for Mr. Mansfield to asperse this country and to misrepresent conditions here in the most glaring fashion. His recall will be the best solution of the very painful situation in which he has placed himself.

I wish to bring this matter to the attention of the Government and to ask if any steps have been taken, or any representations made to the Government at Washington. with a view to securing a correction of these statements, which are grossly misleading and libellous, so far as the province of British Columbia is concerned, and, I believe, are wilfully and maliciously false.

,Conservative (1867-1942),,Henry Herbert Stevens,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=b2723513-c609-4a5c-87f4-bd7c225ccd75&Language=E&Section=ALL
451148,ca.proc.d.1916-04-27.3.5.3,1916-04-27,896b827c-c49c-4978-9b77-7590d414c5ee,ca.m.7312,Hon. W. J. ROCHE (Minister of the Interior) :,Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior,QUESTIONS.,ALLEGED ENLISTMENT OP FOREIGN LABOURERS.,,Mr. Speaker, this matter was

brought to my personal- attention for the first time yesterday, owing to an article that, I believe, appeared first in the Chicago Tribune as the result of an interview with the United States Immigration Commissioner in that city, based upon a circular which he states he received from Washington to the effect indicated by the hon. member for Vancouver. Immediately on hearing of this article the Superintendent of Immigration communicated with our immigration agent at Vancouver, and asked him to interview the United States Consul General in Vancouver as to the accuracy of the -statements attributed to him. He did so, and the United States Consul General in Vancouver refused to either confirm or deny the statements until he saw the particular specified articles based on the statements attributed to him. Since that time our agent has been more than once communicated with, and asked to again interview the Consul General- in Van-

couver, and to obtain his confirmation or denial. The statements contained in the article are certainly not warranted by the facts, or by the conditions in the province of British Columbia. We have communicated, also, with, the United States Immigration Commissioner in Montreal, who does not at all agree with such articles,' and has communicated his views on the matter to his Government at Washington. I understand that a circular was sent out from Washington, said to be based upon reports made by the Consul General located at Vancouver, but as far as unemployment is concerned in British Columbia and Vancouver, our reports are to the effect that comparatively little unemployment existed there. During January and' February, which would be the most likely months, in the midst of winter, for unemployment to prevail, only 285 individuals had applied to the city for relief. This is not more than a normal number during any winter in normal times, in a city the size of Vancouver. I should be very sorry, indeed, to think that the consul representing the United States in Vancouver would be the author o.f these misrepresentations:, and it is only right to afford him a final opportunity of denying or confirming the statements, which, no doubt, by this time have been placed before him. We have had a great demand in western Canada, as well as in eastern Canada, for farm labourers, and the propaganda we have been carrying on in the United States in order to secure these men has been twisted and distorted 'by interested parties in the United States, to prevent their people from migrating to Canada, warning them that if they came to this country they would most likely be subject to conscription, and might be pressed into the army for war purposes. Such are the representations we have had to contend against in the United States for some time past. However, in a day or so, probably to-morrow, we shall have fuller information on the subject. In the meantime we are endeavouring to correct this erroneous impression.

,Conservative (1867-1942),,William James Roche,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=896b827c-c49c-4978-9b77-7590d414c5ee&Language=E&Section=ALL

451167,ca.proc.d.1916-04-27.3.8.8,1916-04-27,a10e65bf-4275-4011-8604-14dde37cf065,ca.m.9749,Sir THOMAS WHITE:,Minister of Finance and Receiver General,QUESTIONS.,BOUNTIES ON ZINC.,,I do not quite

understand the point my hon. friend is making. The bounty will apply when the price of zinc in cakes, blocks, or pigs falls below 8 cents per pound. Then there is a provision that the zinc or spelter shall contain not more than two per cent of impurities. It must be produced in Canada and the zinc ores must be mined in Canada. The price of zinc in cakes, Blocks, or pigs is higher than the price of zinc in sheets, and it is only when the higher price falls below 8 cents per pound that the bounty will apply, and then it is to be paid upon zinc or spelter containing not more than 2 per cent of impurities, and produced in Canada.

451174,ca.proc.d.1916-04-27.4.2.1,1916-04-27,a10e65bf-4275-4011-8604-14dde37cf065,ca.m.9749,Sir THOMAS WHITE:,Minister of Finance and Receiver General,SUPPLY.,,,"When this item was under consideration last evening, the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) asked me to place upon Hansard an explanation of it. My deputy minister has given me this memorandum on the subject:

In the Supplementary Estimates for the fiscal year ended 31st March, 1916, recently brought down in the House, there is an item [DOT] "" To cover unprovided items 1914-15 as per Auditor General's Report, Part B, page 3, 1914-15 $228,664.18.""

At the end of each fiscal year, when the expenditures under the innumerable appropriations are finally adjusted, it has always been found that here and there throughout the service there have been small over-expenditures. These are all reported in the Auditor General's Report as indicated in the item above, and a sum inserted in the supplementary estimates at the next session to legalize the total amount of these over-expenditures. While in the total appropriations of a department there may be large amounts unexpended, if there is any over-expenditure in a sub-head of the total vote, such over-expenditure is reported by the Auditor General.

The total amount of $228,664.18 is made up of amounts from 43 cents upward. In large and varied services these over-expenditures are discovered too late to enable a supplementary estimate to be taken for the year's accounts in which the outlay has been made. For example, in the accounts of 1914-15, which were not closed until long after the session of 1915, it was impossible to get a supplementary estimate at the time the over-expenditure was discovered. Frequently, too, the circumstances change between the taking of an estimate, and the expenditures occur in such a way as to effect the sub-votes to which an outlay is
charged. The unprovided items are all set forth in detail in the Auditor General's Report, as indicated in the vote in the Supplementary Estimates.
With this explanation the item might be allowed to pass.

,Conservative (1867-1942),,William Thomas White,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=a10e65bf-4275-4011-8604-14dde37cf065&Language=E&Section=ALL
451175,ca.proc.d.1916-04-27.4.2.2,1916-04-27,a10e65bf-4275-4011-8604-14dde37cf065,ca.m.9749,Sir THOMAS WHITE:,Minister of Finance and Receiver General,SUPPLY.,,,The hon. member tor South Renfrew asked that this item be allowed to stand until to-day. I pointed out last night that provision had been made for maintenance only. A question was asked, I think by the hon. member for St. John, as to why there was an increase in this item. I might point out that the Estimates for 1915-16 included an item of $100,000 to be expended in laying out and constructing a park on the battlefields of Quebec, and other items covering expenses of administration, and maintenance of the Battlefields park and of the Martello tower. This year, on account of the burden of the war and the desire to keep expenses within bounds, we have asked the Battlefields Commission to curtail their expenses as much as is reasonably possible, and as a result we have the estimate contained in this item. It is not the intention of the commission, I understand, to acquire new property during the coming year.

,Conservative (1867-1942),,William Thomas White,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=a10e65bf-4275-4011-8604-14dde37cf065&Language=E&Section=ALL
451176,ca.proc.d.1916-04-27.4.2.3,1916-04-27,e2f3ce71-bd81-4d34-8a08-56a140552231,ca.m.3549,Sir WILFRID LAURIER:,Leader of the Official Opposition,SUPPLY.,,,This commission has done excellent work so far, and work of extreme importance towards preserving the history of the Plains of Abraham. Every stranger coming to Quebec inquires where Wolfe's army landed, -and where the battle took place. At present it is impossible to get access to the spot where Wolfe's army landed, because you have to go through private property belonging now to Les Dames de la Congregation. I know that the commission has it in mind to acquire a piece of property on which to construct a road along the cliff up to Wolfe's Cove, where the troops landed and climbed up to the Plains. Of course this will cost money, but not very much, and although we must economize in those times, I think my hon. friend will agree with me that the longer We postpone acquiring this property, the more we may have to pay for it. I hope my hon. friend will place in his next Estimates the small sum necessary to acquire, that land.

,Liberal,,Wilfrid Laurier,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=e2f3ce71-bd81-4d34-8a08-56a140552231&Language=E&Section=ALL
451177,ca.proc.d.1916-04-27.4.2.4,1916-04-27,a10e65bf-4275-4011-8604-14dde37cf065,ca.m.9749,Sir THOMAS WHITE:,Minister of Finance and Receiver General,SUPPLY.,,,I am very glad indeed to have the benefit of the views of my right hon. friend, and I shall be very glad to give the matter my attention. After

all, a few thousand dollars is neither here nor there in Dominion finance, and I am entirely in sympathy with having the work completed. As my right hon. friend says, the place to which he has referred is historic, and there is no desire on my part to curtail the work of the commission. On the contrary I have supported them ever since I have been minister, and our relations have been entirely satisfactory. I had the opportunity some time ago of going over the work, and I was very much impressed with what had been done. I shall be very glad to see whether we cannot act upon my right hon. friend's representations.

That item has Deen in the Estimates for five or six years. A wharf at that point, which is intended as a shipping place for vessels carrying cargoes to and from Charlo's cove and Larry's river, as well as 'Cole harbour, is very much needed by the people of that locality. I have drawn the attention of the minister, and also of his predecessor, to the necessity of building this wharf. Every year since my hon. friend's party has been in power I have inquired about this matter, and I was told on various occasions that the work would be attended to later. They say that the Sultan of Turkey is not very easily moved in the matter of granting reforms. When the young Turks ask for changes in the 'Government and improvements in the administration they usually get the answer : "" Please God, to-morrow."" That is the kind of answer I have been getting from the minister, and his predecessor, in connection with this important work. I hope that this item will not remain in the Estimates forever without being spent. It is the only item in my constituency that has appeared in the Estimates for a number of years. I represent

one of the largest fishing counties in the province of Nova Scotia, where improvements on the coast are very much needed. Any improvements that have been carried out, though not great in number, have been of great service. Some works were built by the late Government that have been of considerable advantage to the fishermen on that stormy coast, giving them protection from the sea for their boats and a steamer service to take their products to market. My hon. friend can hardly realize the importance of a small wharf to this district; 1 am afraid he does not realise what harm he is doing to the progress of that country by not going on with important works of this kind. This is the only item for that county that the minister has been generous enough to retain in the estimates. Most of them were put in before his party came into power, and afterwards were ruthlessly struck out without any explanation and without any promise of doing anything in the future. ,Fo,r some reason this item ihas remained in the estimates, but the money has never been spent. I know that the minister's department is scarce of money, but small expenditures are made in most of the counties and I would suggest to him that this amount would not be too much to spend to afford facilities to this long line of coast which are so much needed by the fishermen of that locality.

451382,ca.proc.d.1916-04-27.4.2.209,1916-04-27,651714ed-1fa2-4874-a656-3e55434ef8cc,ca.m.535,Mr. COPP:,,SUPPLY.,,,I wish to bring to the minister's attention the unfortunate position in which Sackville is placed in regard to wharf accommodation. We have had very poor wharf accommmodation there for a number of years. A great effort was made to induce the Government to make some repairs, or to build a new wharf. About 1909 or 1910 w;e got an appropriation and a new wharf was constructed at a point some distance from the site of the old wharf, which had practically tumbled down so that it was impossible for vessels to tie up at it. At the time of the construction of the new wharf there was some friction, as is usually the case where there is any change in the site of a wharf. However,

the wharf was constructed on the new site, 400 yards lower down the stream, at a point where there is a sharp bend, so it is possible for vessels to start out into the stream so as to avoid the difficulty of making the sharp curve in the river on a strong tide. Something like $40,000 was expended, and a very splendid wharf was constructed at this site. It was about completed at the time of the change of Government. A few people in the town were small enough to allow their politics to influence them to oppose any road being made to the wharf, and for some time we had no road. Finally a road was constructed to the wharf. But there is still no railroad accommodation. The result is that last year or the year before some pressure was brought to bear upon the Government and they made some small repairs to the old wharf, but these repairs were only sufficient to enable small vessels to come to the old wharf. The result is that captains in charge of large coasting vessels that formerly came to Sack-ville and delivered and took on cargoes, refused to go there owing to the lack of proper wharf accommodation. It is impossible to ship out timber from the old wharf or to handle the large amount of timber that formerly came in by that wharf, going to the adjoining town of Amherst. We have really mo wharf accommodation, and practically this new wharf is going to pieces without being used.

It seems to me that it is time the Government took this matter up. I think the feeling which arose has been dissipated, and I do not think there would be very strong opposition now from the minister's political friends. It was only -a few who caused the feeling. , Some arrangement should be made between the Department of Public Works and the Department of Railways and Canals so that that wharf, which was intended for the public service, should give the people in that community some advantage for the money that was expended upon it some years ago. Under present conditions it is not worth a five-cent piece to the people of Sackville.

A very enterprising American firm from Philadelphia has started there a very large industry, the manufacture of sulphide pulp. I visited the place last summer. They are employing some 800 men at the mills, and I understand that they intend to double that number in the course of the coming year. The pier in question was begun a few years ago. There was an old pier which is used by the fishermen, but the new pier, which was commenced, has not yet been completed. The intention of the company is to ship the pulp from that point. At present, thanks to the Gaspe railway, they ship their pulp from Gaspe basin. This means to them a large expenditure, but they were very pleased to use what facilities they had at Gaspe to ship their pulp to the United States where they have large orders to fill This company has built during the last two years 12 or 15 miles of a railway which goes deep into the woods, and they have built their line as far as the present landing pier. I called the attention of the minister some time ago to the fact that until last year the vessels which they used could anchor near that pier. With the trade increasing as it has increased during the last few months, this pier should certainly be extended. There is an alternative plan, and the engineer of the Department was kind enough to ask the company to point out which of the two would be more in their interests, and I understand their answer will be given shortly. The

I think the Government would do well to consider whether it would not be more in the interest of all parties concerned to accept the plan suggested by the company, rather than that of the engineer of the department. 451429,ca.proc.d.1916-04-27.4.4.23,1916-04-27,a5a56521-a20b-4265-a2ac-40ae006805ca,ca.m.3795,Mr. ROGERS:,Minister of Public Works,SUPPLY.,,,I appreciate the remarks of my hon. friend in respect to the question before the committee. This, as my hon. friend well knows, is a very important work. It is the main highway between New York and Montreal, and other points, the main highway over which all people travel with their automobiles between the United States and Montreal. I must confess that this very important undertaking has .not been carried out as I had hoped that it would be and as I certainly believe that it should have been. In my opinion the blame should be attached not so much to the contractors as .to the engineers who made faulty plans in connection with the undertaking and who have been dismissed for the mistakes they made in connection with the preparation of these plans. I shall be glad to give my hon. friend all the information that I possibly can. I understand that the amendment asked for in the Estimates is quite sufficient to complete the work and make it a very passable highway, satisfactory to all. The estimated cost of completing the work is as follows: Plans on price of contract, $23,600.46; plans on agreement of temporary road, $850; rebuilding of inner wall, $11,000. (That is the part that gave way through the faulty plan of the engineer, this

causing the difficulty and trouble which arose); erecting the parapet, $23,000; three additional culverts, $5,000; additional inclined roadways, $11,000; extra for asphalted macadam $5,400, a total of $79,850.46. In view of the fact that this dyke is a link of a very important international highway, extensively used by tourists from Canada and the United States, the roadway on top of the dyke cannot be opened to the public until the whole of the work has been completed. This dyke is being built in order to protect the town of Laprairie against heavy annual damages caused by ice shoves and floods, and also to afford better communication with Montreal. These floods have been caused, at least partially, by the construction of different public works which have had the effect of narrowing the flowing section of the St. Lawrence below Laprairie, such as the Victoria bridge abutments and piers, the Mackay guard pier, and the Verdun dyke. The total estimated cost of the work is $158,953. The total amount paid to the contractors up to August 18, 1915 is $56,920. Work on the contract was stopped owing to lack of funds, the vote of $20,000 made last session having been used partly for the construction of a temporary plank road, pending the completion of the contract. The work done during the past fiscal year consisted of the following: (a) 700 feet of the 15-foot road bed was laid and 2,226 tons of crushed stone delivered on the site of the work. Inspector, A. Dufort, at $3 per day. (b) A macadamized roadway, 6,500 feet long, was constructed in order to temporarily accommodate the traffic during the spring season. Stones, already delivered, were spread on the work and covered with crushed stone. Foreman, Roch Lefebvre, at $3 per day. (c) Construction of a plank roadway alongside the dyke for a length of 6,500 feet. This was necessary in order to accommodate the traffic during the construction of the dyke. An Order in Council was passed, December 4, 1913, granting authority to accept the tender of Messrs. Alphonse Duranceau and Noe Poupart, of Laprairie, Que., at unit prices (entailing an approximate expenditure of $72,678.73) for the construction of a protection dyke at Laprairie, Que. Contract No. 9,909, amount $72,678.73 (schedule of prices); contractors, Duranceau, A., and Poupart, Noe, Laprairie, Que., date of contract, January 21, 1914; date of completion, 18 months from 6th December, 1913. The Department of Public Works decided to commence the

construction of this work with the last 1,400 feet (the wholle work comprising 8,000 feet) and to have this length of the dyke completed within six weeks from the notification of the acceptance of the tender, the intention being to connect, this fall, the provincial road from where it ends along the route of the King Edward highway, as laid out, with the point where it joins the Old Road. This temporary roadway was necessary to accommodate the traffic during the construction of the dyke which was being built on the existing roadway.
District Engineer Michaud, in a report dated 18th April, 1913, states as follows:

In 1910, the Government decided that some steps should he taken to improve these conditions, and the sum of $10,000 was expended to raise the shore road six feet above its ordinary-level from the town of Laprairie towards St. Lambert and use this dyke as a roadway. 3,000 feet of this was filled with earth and riprapped on the shore slope during the year 1910-11.

During the fiscal years 1911-12 and 1912-13, the work was continued and mostly completed for a distance of 7,900 feet to an average height of 13 feet above extreme low water. The shore side of the dyke was partly riprapped and cemented.
The flood of the spring 1913, which was 4 feet above this protection dyke, scored out the side slope which had not been riprapped, and damaged the road bed generally to a great extent.

In order to ensure a greater protection and build a more permanent dyke which must necessarily be the highway out of the town ^ of Laprairie during the flood period, and a link of the King Edward VII Road from Rousse's Point to Montreal, which is undertaken by the Provincial Government with the aid of interested municipalities, the work already performed should be considerably extended. It will be necessary to raise the dyke 4 feet above its present level, macadamize the top on a width of 24 feet riprap and cement both slopes in order to secure permanency of all surfaces exposed to flood.
'''All the low shore exposed on the Laprairie basin for a length of 7,900 feet would be permanently protected, and free access in all times of the year would be provided for the town.

Quebec, 21st October, 1913. The Hon. Ilobert Rogers,
Minister of Public Works,
Ottawa.
Hear Sir,

Will you let me call your attention to the fact that there is still a large amount of work to be done, to complete that portion of the King Edward V11 road under the control of your department in the parish of Laprairie.
No work of any importance has been done this summer and there is no probability that the road will be completed for the beginning of the summer of 1914.

It is not my purpose to reflect in any manner on the reasons which have prevented the work to proceed during the last summer. I wish only to state that the provincial part of the road is very near completion now and will probably be finished in two weeks time if we have fair weather.

The provincial government has spent a large sum upon this road and we are very anxious to have it completed for the beginning of next year,, in order to accommodate the large tourist travel which will come from the border.
I thought that perhaps you would welcome an .offer from my department to complete the road next spring. We have five of our outfits on the ground. Our contractor is there also with a large plant.

I think we could finish the embankment this fall and easily complete your part of the road for the end of June next if your department is willing to enter into an agreement as to the cost with my own department.
I am sure that you sincerely desire to complete this road as soon as possible and we are ready ourselves to co-operate with your department to attain this end if you care to consider our proposition.
Truly yours,
(Sgd) Jos. Ed. Caron.
Office of the Minister of Public Works of Canada, Ottawa,
My dear sir,
October 27, 191-3.

I have your letter of the 21st instant -, in reference to the construction of the King, Edward VII road in the parish of Laprairie, and in reply to the same I might state that the department called for tenders for this work recently and that a recommendation is now before council to award the contract. The contractor undertakes to perform the work in question this fall. Were it not that the proceedings had reached this stage I would have been pleased to take up with your department the work in question.
Your sincerely,
(Sgd) R. Rogers.
Hon. Joseph D. Caron,
Quebec, P.Q.

This amount of $150,000 is required to continue the harbour improvements at Rimouski. The improvements consist of a timber structure filled with stone, built parallel to the western and northern face of the present wharf, the whole length of the cribwork aggregating 1,458 feet, to be seated, in a trench previously dredged to a depth of 25 feet below low water the dredging of a tidal basin 1,100 feet by 600 feet to a depth 25 feet below low water ; and the filling of the space between the old and hew works. Estimated cost, $350,000'. This work will promote the development of trade in the district. Several important saw, pulp, and other mills are greatly in need of these improvements to facilitate their shipping trade. These improvements will also procure deep water accommodation and shelter for vessels frequenting the harbour and will make Rimouski a very good port of refuge, being protected by St. Barnabe Island and by the wharf. The work was requested by the Board of Trade of Rimouski in a resolution dated
February, 1912.

column2: (Translation.) Mr. Chairman, I wonder whether my hon. friend from'Bonaventure (Mr. Marcil) has grasped the question. I fail +o -see on what grounds he finds exorbitant the expenditure now being made in the harbour of Rimouski; for he knows just as well as I do that it is one of the most important harbours on the lower St. Lawrence.

column1: For many years past, the port of Rimouski has been the centre of an active trade in lumber, and the proposed improvements would enable ships to load right -at the wharf. Heretofore, ships had to take on their cargo of lumber three or four miles away from the wharf, which entailed on the shippers the use of lighters. It is known, besides, that the Price Company has several establishments in the counties of Matane and Rimouski, and, every year, several of their

vessels are plying to and from the port of Rimouski. Here is therefore a requirement of the lumber trade. As regards the mail boats, even should these improvements be carried to completion, they would still be unable to reach the Rimouski wharf; to attain that object, some dredging and deepening of the channel would be necessary. Then again, those improvements would allow of vessels such as the Lady Evelyn, for example, with a draft of twenty feet, and which lands the mails and passengers from the transatlantic steamers, to reach the wharf under all conditions of tide. Moreover, the contract was granted previous to the outbreak of the war, and the work must he carried through. My hon. friend from Bonaventure was not so particular, when his friends were in power, about requesting the construction of wharves in his constituency at distances of every four or five miles. He is not in a position to obtain such favours just now, and that explains the bitterness of his remarks.

The people of the county of Rimouski have been neglected for a number of years, and it is only right that this Government should see to it that we are protected and that we get the improvements which the trade has been in need of for so long a time.

This dam was constructed to regulate the discharge of Lake Nipissing, so that during the fall or low months the water level of the lake may be maintained about elevation 643-5 or about half way between mean summer level and high-water. This will serve the purpose of facilitating the handling of the logs at the different mills on the lake, and also provide a constant depth at the various wharves and harbours where the department has made improvements by dredging. A contract for this work was awarded to J. F. Boyd of Sault Ste. Marie, in January 1911; contract price $13,365, but he gave up his contract in November, 1912. The work was completed by the department and the dam in working order by the first of October, 1913. Total cost of dam at Little ChaudiOre Rapids, $27,719.77. The only departmental work in the locality is the French River Dam Big Chaudiere, about 5 miles away. This dam is at present under construction. The French River dam is situated across the west channel of the Little Chaudiere rapids at the outlet of Lake Nipissing into French River. There is no town near the site of the dam. The nearest towns are Sturgeon Falls and North Bay, each about 42 miles distant.

When that report was made, it might have been justified, but I do not think it will be justified now. My information is that the company intend during

the coming summer to employ in the vicinity of 500 men, so that the work would be entirely justified. Some few years ago a wharf was built there by the Government, and I understand that this vote is simply for repairs. I would like if the minister would reconsider the matter, because I think it would be quite a disappointment to these capitalists if they found that the Government was not disposed to give them any encouragement even to the extent of repairing a Government wharf. The result, I am sure, will be that they will have to spend the money themselves, because they have the capital; they are arranging for a large development, and they are actually at work to-day. They will require to take in a large quantity of machinery which, of course, they cannot take in unless they have wharf accommodation. Perhaps the minister would allow the item to stand, and then he can treat it like other items and go on with the work or not, as he may be advised later. I am sure my hon. friend from Vancouver (Mr. Stevens) has heard of the company which is proceeding to operate now on a very large scale.

,Conservative (1867-1942),,Robert Rogers,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=a5a56521-a20b-4265-a2ac-40ae006805ca&Language=E&Section=ALL
451755,ca.proc.d.1916-04-27.4.4.349,1916-04-27,b443ed18-8c97-4f61-a408-a844789acb40,ca.m.6066,Mr. HUGHES:,,SUPPLY.,,,For instance, the company gets the services of operators free, for the railway station masters act as operators, and the only compensation given is that the telegraph company carries the railway messages free. In the town where I live the company is so economical that they will not even provide a boy to carry the telegraph messages, but the railway officials have to deliver the messages whenever they get time from their regular duties. I should think that a company that is receiving so many advantages ought to be compelled to give a better service. And when the last train has left-I think the latest train is about six o'clock-the station master closes his office and you cannot get a message through afterwards. Sometimes he generously keeps the office open when he knows that there is business to be done, but the company give him nothing for the extra work. I call the special attention of the minister to that. I think something should be done to compel the company to give a better service. At Charlottetown, perhaps, they give a service more suitable to the place, and at Summerside. But at Souris, for instance, where there is a good deal of business done and where a considerable portion of the time of the railway officials is taken up with telegraphic work, as I have pointed out the company will not even provide a boy to deliver messages but throws that work all upon the railway officials.
